text: The Center for Internet Security publishes a separate, numbered foundations benchmark for Azure and for AWS. Neither one is vague best-practice advice — every recommendation is specific and testable, like requiring multi-factor authentication for privileged users. Together they're the practical output of the last lesson's idea: one control intent, written out twice, once in each cloud's own vocabulary.

Look at how a recommendation is actually structured. CIS Azure Foundations 1.1 requires MFA for privileged users: the rationale is that privileged accounts are the highest-value target in the environment, the audit procedure checks Entra ID security defaults or Conditional Access policies, and the remediation is enabling a Conditional Access policy that requires it. The AWS equivalent, requiring MFA on the root user, has the identical three-part shape — rationale, a concrete audit command, and a remediation step — just aimed at a different identity.

Before you run a single scan, decide which profile you're targeting. Level 1 recommendations are baseline configurations with minimal impact on performance or usability — nearly every organization implements all of them as non-negotiable. Level 2 recommendations go further into real defense-in-depth, with actual operational tradeoffs like stricter default-deny network rules, so you adopt those deliberately, based on your organization's actual risk tolerance, not by default.

A baseline only matters if something keeps you on it. Microsoft Defender for Cloud ships the CIS Microsoft Azure Foundations Benchmark as a built-in regulatory compliance standard, scoring your environment continuously. AWS Security Hub does the same for the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. And where a posture tool measures drift, Azure Policy and AWS Config rules go further and actively enforce it — denying a non-compliant storage account at creation time instead of just flagging it after the fact.

That's a mature baseline: a CIS profile you deliberately chose, wired into a tool that measures it continuously, backed by policy enforcement that stops violations before they ever become a finding. Next lesson picks up exactly there, looking at what a CSPM tool's secure score is actually built from underneath the number you see on the dashboard.
